pg009_p020: Keeping records of cash and banking transactions is essential for everyone.
pg009_p021: To manage your pocket money properly, you must keep some records of your transactions. Businesses have systems to record receipts and payments of cash and banking transactions that form part of their day-to-day operations. In this chapter, you will learn the meaning of cash and banking transactions, the types of cash book, and preparation of cash books (single-column, two-column, three-column, and the petty cash books). The competencies developed will enable you to record cash and banking transactions in different types of cash books appropriately.

pg010_p008: Banking transactions refer to financial transactions that involve the flow of money into or out of a customer’s, or business’s bank account. pg010_p025: Banking transactions provide a safe and secure way to handle money. They reduce the risk of loss or theft associated with holding cash. They also offer accurate record-keeping of transactions, which helps individuals and businesses to track their revenues and expenses effectively.

pg029_p055: A three-column cash book is a cash book that is prepared with three amount columns on both sides (debit and the credit). It has one additional column from the two-column cash book. The third column is designed to record cash discount. The three-column cash book is, therefore, a cash book with three amount columns, namely: the cash column, bank column and discount column. When a business has more than one bank account, each account will have a separate column, but the cash book will still be known as the three-column cash book.

pg037_p025: The word petty means small. A petty cash book is a separate cash book specifically maintained to record small cash payments, also known as petty payments. This book is usually operated by a specific cashier known as petty cashier. The petty cash book records petty payments such as office expenses, postage, telephone, stationeries, cleaning expenses, sundry expenses using columns that are designed to each category of expenses that the business may pay for using the petty cash fund. Petty cash cannot be used to purchase non-current assets, because they usually require large amount. When preparing the petty cash system, the business would normally have a policy that states which types of payments are settled with petty cash fund. The policy should state the limit of the amount of any single payment to be made through petty cash as well as the petty cash period. The petty cash period is the period between
pg037_p048: receiving the petty cash float and petty cash replenishment.
pg037_p051: The petty cash system works where the main cashier delegates petty cash payments to the petty cashier. The petty cashier is therefore provided with an agreed amount of cash known as petty cash float for the purpose of making petty cash payments. The cashier continues to use the petty cash for making various payments and records the transactions until the end of the period, or until the amount is finished. At the end of this, the petty cashier submits the details of payments and relevant source documents to the main cashier. The main cashier then makes a replenishment of the amount spent so that a new petty cash period can begin. The replenishment of the petty cash float is known as reimbursement.
pg037_p069: This kind of operation is known as an imprest system, and the petty cash float is also referred to as imprest amount.
pg038_p003: The name imprest is historically associated with a Latin word ‘imprestare’, meaning
pg038_p005: ‘to lend’. Imprest sytem works not only for processing petty cash transactions, but also other business for larger transactions.
pg038_p008: The imprest system for petty cash is the system in which the petty cashier periodically receives a specified amount of cash from chief cashier. The petty cashier will be required to maintain all the documents (vouchers and receipts) that evidence payment from such amount and the amount to be restored by the chief cashier. In other words, the chief cashier
pg038_p017: ‘lends’ the petty cashier a specific amount of cash for use in various cash transactions.
pg038_p019: It remains as an imprest (loan) until evidence in terms of documents (petty cash vouchers and receipts) is submitted to the chief cashier to justify the payments.
pg038_p023: Ideally, the petty cashier will have to refund the money to the chief cashier when he or she fails to provide evidence
pg038_p027: Traditionally, many businesses use the petty cash voucher (abbreviated as PCV) as a source document for payments from the petty cash, although the PCV can be complemented with receipts or other documents from third parties.

pg069_p034: These errors are unilateral; meaning that the error is made in one of the accounts involved in recording the transaction.
pg069_p037: In case, it is a casting error in balancing an account, the entry to correct will be crediting (provided that the casting error increased debit balance or reduced a credit balance). The vice versa is also true.
pg069_p042: The entry required to correct an error which affects trial balance does not necessarily require double entry as was the case with errors that do not affect trial balance agreement. Instead, the corresponding entries for these errors are made in a temporary account opened for special purpose. This account is called a suspense account.
pg069_p052: A suspense account is an account that is used to temporarily record a balance that cannot be explained at a particular moment. Traditionally, a suspense account is used by businesses as part of general ledger to record unclear entries that require clarification. A good example is when a business notices a credit entry has been made in its bank statement, meaning that someone has made a deposit in its account. While waiting for clarification of who made the deposit and for what
pg070_p004: purpose, this amount will be placed in a suspense account. Once the clarification is obtained, the amount will be posted to the appropriate general ledger account.
pg070_p008: When the trial balance totals fail to agree, a balance is inserted temporarily in the side with a lower amount of total. Doing so will make the total debit balance and total credit balance to be the same. For example, when the total credit balances is TZS 10,200,000 and the total debit balances is TZS 9,750,000, a debit balance of TZS 450,000 is inserted to make both totals TZS 10,200,000. The account name given to this balance is suspense account.
pg070_p019: When errors that affect the trial balance are corrected, double entry is completed in the suspense account. When all errors have been corrected, the balance in the
pg070_p023: suspense account will be zero. For this reason, a suspense account balance will no longer appear in the trial balance.
pg070_p026: It may also happen that not all errors
pg070_p027: that affect the trial balance agreement have been discovered and corrected at the time when financial statements are being prepared. In this case, the suspense account would still have a balance. When the suspense account exists up to the date
pg070_p033: of preparing the financial statements, the balance would be reflected in the statement of financial position. The balance will be shown as a current asset or current liability, depending on whether it is a debit balance or a credit balance.

pg090_p018: 5. Identifying and correcting errors is crucial for maintaining accurate financial statements and ensuring the reliability of accounting records.

pg105_p010: An uncredited cheque is a cheque which the business has received and deposited into the bank, but the bank has not yet completed clearing the cheque with the drawer’s bank. The amount must have been debited in the cash book when the cheque was lodged to the bank, but will not appear on the credit column of the bank statement until when the respective cheque is cleared. Uncredited cheques are also called uncleared cheques, uncleared deposits or deposits in transit.
pg105_p023: A dishonoured cheque is a cheque that the bank refuses to pay (to honour) for various reasons. Cheques are dishonored for the following reasons:
pg105_p027: (a) The drawer has insufficient funds with the bank, for example, the drawer has a bank balance of TZS

pg105_p032: (b) The cheque has an error(s) on it, for example amount in words differs from the amount in figures.
pg105_p035: (c) It is not signed by the drawer, or the signature does not match the signature in the bank records.
pg105_p038: (d) If the payee has not signed the back of the cheque (endorsed) before presenting it to the bank. For some
pg105_p041: customers, the bank may want the payee or the drawer to stamp on the back of the cheque.
pg105_p044: (e) It is post-dated. A post-dated cheque is presented for payment before the issue date (date written on the cheque). An example of a post-dated cheque is a cheque that the date of drawing or issue is written as 1st June
pg105_p052: (f) It is stale. A stale cheque is a cheque that is presented for payment at a date later than six months from the issue date or from the date it was drawn. An example of a stale cheque is a cheque drawn on 20th September
pg105_p058: 2023 but presented to the bank for payment on 1st April 2024.

pg115_p013: Bank reconciliation statement includes other items, such as errors and dishonoured cheques, when reconciling bank records of a business. Therefore, there is a need to know how to treat such items when adjusting the cash book and preparing a bank reconciliation statement.
pg115_p020: In the case of errors, the treatment depends on the kind of error and its effect on the relationship between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance.
pg115_p024: If the error is in the cash book, it is treated as an adjusting item. It is dealt with when preparing the adjusted cash book.
pg115_p027: It will be treated as a reconciling item if unadjusted cash book balance is used when preparing the bank reconciliation statement.
pg115_p031: On the other hand, if the error is in the bank statement, the usual procedure is to notify the bank so that they can make an entry to reverse the error. Such reversing entry is reflected in the next bank statement. This makes bank reconciliation an important process. While waiting for the rectified bank statement, the amount of the error will be treated as a reconciling item.
pg115_p040: As for a dishonoured cheque, it is important to consider two possible sides.
pg115_p042: One is where the cheque dishonoured is a cheque that the business has received and deposited with its banks. Another side is the case where the cheque is the one that the business has issued to its creditor and for one reason or another it is dishonoured by the bank. Cheques received or issued when dishonoured are further clarified in the following subsections.
pg115_p052: This is the case where the business has received a cheque from a customer and deposited it with its bank. Apart from noticing that it has not been credited in the bank statement when comparing the bank statement and the cash book, the business would also receive a notification from the bank that the cheque is dishonoured.
pg115_p060: The cheque will also be returned to the business, which can make further reference from the customer. In any case, the dishonored cheque will be treated as an adjusting item. This is because the cheque will have to be cancelled by the customer, who will issue a fresh cheque to the business for the intended payment.
pg115_p068: The cash book adjustment necessary for this dishonoured cheque is a credit entry.
pg115_p070: This is because the amount must have been debited in the cash book when this cheque was originally deposited into the bank.
pg115_p075: When the business issued the cheque, it must have credited the cash book. The problem could have started when the payee presented the cheque for payment.
pg116_p003: When a cheque is dishonoured, it would not be debited in the bank statement. After dealing with the problem that led to the dishonour, the business will have to cancel the cheque and issue a fresh one. The entry for cancelling the cheque is to debit the cash book when adjusting it.

pg139_p025: Cash flow planning: A cash budget helps individuals or businesses to predict cash flows (inflows and outflows) to ensure liquidity.
pg139_p029: Planning for money: A budget helps businesses and individuals to understand how much money they will receive from different sources and how much they will spend to operate a business in the future.
pg139_p034: This enables them to plan for future expenditure such as salaries, electricity bills, and rent. Therefore, without a budget, unexpected expenses can cause financial problems.

pg139_p048: Making good decisions: When a business knows how much money it expects to have in a certain period, it can make better choices about spending and saving. A budget helps to decide whether to expand the business, buy new assets, or reduce expenditures. This avoids overspending and ensures that money is available when needed.
pg139_p057: Controlling costs: A budget enables businesses and individuals to track spending and avoid unnecessary costs.
pg139_p060: Business owners can identify areas of overspending and take steps to control it. This practice helps to save money and enhances financial stability.
